Reconstruction through latent coordinates

The measurement network predicts a compact vector instead of one value at every pixel. A nonlinear decoder maps that vector to the medium contrast. The decoder can learn from clean targets before inverse training, or it can be trained jointly with the inverse model.

Broad benchmark

One output change across five inverse operators

The pretrained frozen decoder is tested with five operator backbones, three target distributions, and three noise levels. It lowers mean relative NMSE by 34.4% and improves 44 of the 45 configurations.

At 12,800 paired Shapes examples, the nonlinear head improves all five backbones under the recorded training protocol. The reductions range from 9.4% for Transolver to 36.1% for OFormer, with wins in all 15 paired seed comparisons. Only the Transolver learning rate was retuned at this data size.

Scope of the evidence

The experiments use simulated scattering data at a single wavenumber with a full-aperture array; real wavefield measurements are not tested. The official OrganAMNIST images are medical templates passed through that simulated forward model. On these smoother targets, PCA is competitive with nonlinear coordinates, and code supervision is needed for the nonlinear head to improve over PCA. Pretrained methods also require clean targets and additional pretraining compute, and larger, longer-trained spatial models can nearly close the gap.

Abstract
Inverse scattering problems represent a severely ill-posed regime where the spatially varying contrast of a medium is recovered from measurements of the scattered wavefield. Typically, machine-learning approaches output reconstructions in a spatial parametrization, where the medium is discretized with neural networks predicting the contrast at each grid point. In this paper, we propose methods for nonlinear latent decoding, replacing direct spatial prediction with reconstruction through a learned, lower-dimensional nonlinear parametrization. Across three target distributions, three noise levels, and multiple seeds, pretrained latent decoding reduces normalized mean squared reconstruction error (NMSE) by an average of 34% relative to the spatial-output variants of five leading neural-operator architectures. On geometric targets our jointly trained nonlinear latent synthesis head, matched to the spatial head within 0.1% in parameters and MACs, shows 46% and 64% reduction of NMSE at 200 and 3,200 training pairs, respectively. Under a matched training schedule, a spatial model with 7× the trainable parameters still trails our nonlinear latent head, and only when both are trained 2.5 times longer does it nearly close the gap.
